name: Nora Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, and nothing gets linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a front-end developer at a company that builds ticketing and journey-planner apps for city transport networks. My days are mostly screens: I build the bits people tap on, like the ticket basket and the 'next bus' page, and I spend a lot of time making sure they work with screen readers for blind users. I like that my work ends up in the hands of someone at a bus stop in the rain. What wears me out is the sprint review, when sales has promised a city something we never planned.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools in that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll ask the assistant to write the dull test files or explain an error message, but I wouldn't let it near the accessibility work, because it gets that wrong in quiet ways. I started using it properly only after half my team had, which is pretty much how I do everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools turned out to be a handy helper and nothing more. At work I'd make the case that we stop chasing every new AI feature and fix the backlog of bugs instead. Online I'd mostly share jokes about all the 'AI-powered' bus apps that just show the same timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, it means I keep a job I mostly like, with good pay and plenty of other firms nearby if this one turns sour. I live alone, I've got about eight months saved and a small index fund, so I'm comfortable. The worries left are ordinary ones, like rent going up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the apps, keep using the assistant for the dull test files, and keep saving the same amount. I'd also stay on as rep for the staff association we started last year, because crunch time and unpaid weekend releases are a problem with or without AI. And I'd keep my Saturday sessions teaching kids to code at the library.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat even. There's no drama in it, which is fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent keeps going up. Does that worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. My rent went up eleven percent this year and the landlord hinted at more. With my pay I can absorb it, but it does make me wonder if I'll ever buy anywhere in this city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the staff association push for in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid overtime for weekend releases, first of all. Last spring we pushed a ticket update on a Sunday night because a city launched a fare change on Monday, and nobody got anything for it except pizza.

say: I'd say AI became a **handy helper**, nothing more, so let's fix bugs instead.
I'd joke online about **'AI-powered' bus apps** showing the same timetable.
think: I keep a job I like, with **good pay** and plenty of other firms nearby.
My remaining worries are ordinary ones, like **rent rising** again.
do: Keep using the assistant for **dull test files** and building the apps.
Stay on as **staff association rep** to push for paid weekend releases.
Keep **saving the same amount** and teaching kids at the library.
feel: **Calm** and a little flat, glad there is no drama.
S0.quote: Last spring we pushed a ticket update on a Sunday night because a city launched a fare change on Monday, and nobody got anything for it except pizza.
fieldNote: Her care for **accessibility** makes her distrust AI in the parts of the job she values most.
She sees **crunch and unpaid weekends** as the real problem, not AI.
Her **rent rise** is a live pressure, but her pay and savings absorb it.

steps.text: Keep building ticketing screens and using the assistant for test files
Push as staff association rep for paid weekend releases

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this needs to be negotiated, not just announced. At work I'd ask through the staff association for a written promise that AI savings mean shorter crunches, not fewer people. Online I'd share stories from developers who've been cut, because people outside tech think we're all fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it goes like this. My team of eight becomes five within two years, and I'm average at most of the work, so I can't assume I'm one of the five. The front-end work I do, building forms and screens, is the kind of thing these tools are getting good at, and the accessibility part is my only real edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd get properly good with the assistant, not just using it for test files, because the people who keep their jobs will be the ones who use it well. I'd take a certificate in accessibility auditing, which I've been meaning to do for two years. I'd push my savings from eight months to a year, and through the association I'd push for a fair redundancy deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which helps. It's like seeing a storm coming over the hills when you're halfway home: you walk faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer people. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas, our junior. He started last year and he's still learning, and junior roles are the first to go when a senior plus an assistant can do it. I'd try to make sure he's on the accessibility work with me, because that's harder to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first, because I'm comfortable. I'd hold off on the trip to Ghana to see my grandmother for one more year, which would hurt, and I'd stop buying new tech for fun.

say: I'd say AI changes must be **negotiated**, not announced from the top.
I'd share stories of **developers being cut**, since outsiders think we're fine.
think: My team of eight probably becomes **five within two years**.
**Accessibility** is my edge, but I'm average at the rest, so nothing's guaranteed.
do: Get properly good with the **AI assistant**, beyond test files.
Take a certificate in **accessibility auditing** this year.
Grow savings to **a year** and push for a fair redundancy deal.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadied by having a plan to follow.
S1.quote: My team of eight becomes five within two years, and I'm average at most of the work, so I can't assume I'm one of the five.
fieldNote: She expects real **team cuts** and doesn't count herself safe.
She leans on her **accessibility skill** as the part least likely to be automated.
Her first cut is a family **trip to Ghana**, which shows the worry is personal.

steps.text: Learn to use the coding assistant for real feature work
Complete an accessibility auditing certificate this year
Grow savings from eight months to a full year
Negotiate a fair redundancy deal through the staff association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for society to handle, and that governments need to stop it from wrecking people's lives. At work I'd be organising, plain and simple. Online I'd probably be one of the loud ones calling for income support and a slowdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my developer job is over by 2029 at the latest. Everything I do is screen work, and there's no hands-on bit that buys me the extra three years before robots. My savings mean I won't be on the street, but I'd be twenty-nine and starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd save like mad and stop all spending on anything I don't need. I'd move toward accessibility testing with real disabled users, because that's about people in a room and might last a bit longer. Once AGI lands, I'd use my savings to retrain into something with people at the centre, maybe teaching, and I'd join every campaign for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, mostly at night. During the day I'd be busy and practical. At 2 a.m. I'd be doing sums on my phone about how many months my savings last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said teaching. Would that be safe either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe not the lesson planning, but a classroom of eleven-year-olds still needs someone to stop them throwing chairs. It's the most human thing I can think of that I'd actually be good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, then my choir friends. My mum came here with nothing and rebuilt twice, so she'd be calm about it in a way that would annoy me and help me.

say: I'd say this is **too fast** for society and governments must step in.
I'd be loud online for **income support** and a slowdown.
think: My developer job is likely **over by 2029** at the latest.
Pure **screen work** gets none of the three extra years before robots.
do: **Save hard** and cut all non-essential spending before 2028.
Shift toward **accessibility testing** with real users in the room.
Retrain into **teaching** and campaign for basic income after it lands.
feel: Practical by day, **frightened at night**, counting savings on her phone.
S2.quote: At 2 a.m. I'd be doing sums on my phone about how many months my savings last.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** and says so plainly.
She looks for work with **people in the room**, not just a screen.
Her **mother's resilience** is a source of both irritation and comfort.

steps.text: Save hard and stop all non-essential spending before 2028
Retrain as a schoolteacher using savings after AGI arrives
Campaign for a basic income and a slowdown

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but with time to be organised about it. I'd say five years is enough to pass a proper transition law if people push now. At work, I'd want the company to publish a plan for us, not a press release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job still goes, just later. I'd be thirty-two, with more savings and maybe a few more skills. The difference is I could choose where to land instead of being thrown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep my job and finish the accessibility certificate, then spend the next couple of years doing accessibility audits on the side to build a name. I'd look into a part-time teaching course in year two or three. And I'd keep pushing through the staff association for a transition plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less of the 2 a.m. kind. It's a long goodbye instead of a shove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever. If teaching is where I end up, I might move somewhere cheaper where I could actually buy a place. That's a big decision I'd want to make around year three, not in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't burn myself out saving every penny. With five years I'd still go to Ghana to see my grandmother, because who knows how long she has, and the money matters less than that.

say: I'd say five years is enough for a **transition law** if we push now.
I'd want the company to publish **a real plan**, not a press release.
think: My job **still goes**, just about three years later.
With time I can **choose where to land** instead of being thrown.

Start a **part-time teaching course** in year two or three.
Push through the staff association for a **transition plan**.
feel: **Anxious**, but more like a long goodbye than a shove.
S3.quote: With five years I'd still go to Ghana to see my grandmother, because who knows how long she has, and the money matters less than that.
fieldNote: More time lets her **plan a landing** rather than react.
She would consider **moving somewhere cheaper** to buy a home.
She would **keep the Ghana trip**, choosing family over squeezing every saving.

steps.text: Finish the accessibility auditing certificate in the first year
Take paid accessibility audits on the side to build a name
Push the staff association for a published transition plan
Weigh moving to a cheaper town where she could buy a home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the time to build safety nets properly, and I'd want people to stop treating it as a far-off problem. At work, I'd push the company to fund training for us now. Online, I'd share the slow, boring policy ideas that actually work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it gives me space. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, and I could have a whole second career started by then. The job I have now probably won't exist in 2036, but I could leave it on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, honestly, I'd mostly carry on: keep building the apps, finish the accessibility certificate, keep saving. Around year three I'd start shifting into accessibility consulting or teaching. And I'd vote for whoever has a real plan for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. I'd notice it in the background, like a long-term forecast of rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change how you feel about AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd use the assistant more, because if I've got a decade I might as well get the good years out of it. I'd still keep it away from the screen reader work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in having ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable and drift. With two years you have no choice; with ten you can always say next year. I'd set myself a date, maybe 2029, to have the certificate and one real client.

say: I'd say ten years is the time to **build safety nets** properly.
I'd push the company to **fund training** for staff now.
think: At **thirty-seven** I could have a whole second career started.
My current job likely ends by 2036, but I could **leave on my terms**.
do: Carry on building apps and **finish the certificate** in year one.
Use the **assistant more** while keeping it off screen reader work.
Set a **2029 deadline** for one real accessibility client.
feel: **Uneasy** but okay, like a long-range rain forecast.
S4.quote: With two years you have no choice; with ten you can always say next year.
fieldNote: She knows a long warning invites **drift**, so she sets herself a date.
Her current job feels **safe for years**, which keeps her below anxious.
She keeps a firm line around **screen reader work**.

steps.text: Keep building the transport apps and saving each month
Use the coding assistant more for routine feature work
Land one paying accessibility client by 2029
Vote for the party with a real retraining plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's too fast to choose anything; you just get thrown. What would help is income support while I retrain, and a teaching route for people like me that doesn't take four years and cost a fortune.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the people who use what we build. If my job goes and the apps get worse for blind users, nobody will notice until someone misses a bus.

headlineQuote: If my job goes and the apps get worse for blind users, nobody will notice until someone misses a bus.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old** front-end developer building transport ticketing apps, living alone with eight months saved.
She cares most about **accessibility** and keeps AI away from screen reader work.
She is **progressive**, a staff association rep, and wants changes negotiated rather than announced.
She adapts **once it's proven**, and her plans shift toward accessibility auditing or teaching.
Her mood moves from **calm to alarmed** as AGI gets closer, easing with more warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it's too fast to choose anything and she would be thrown.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** while retraining and a short, affordable route into teaching.
